Its performance contexts are mainly tied to Nubian and Shaigiya music in northern Sudan, and it is also used among the Nuba and Beja peoples. The right hand plays the melody with a pick while the left hand sometimes plucks the strings to make a soft drone accompaniment, which shows that it carries both melody and drone in performance. Because the body is a shallow round wooden bowl with a goatskin soundboard, the resonance is warm and slightly nasal, somewhere between the clear ring of the harp and the weight of the pipa. Two soundholes strengthen the middle-frequency resonance and give the sound good projection. In playing, the strings and the wooden resonance of the body mingle, producing a plain, strongly folk sound that is both lyrical and expressive, and particularly suited to delicate melodies and improvisatory passages.

Over time the making and playing of the instrument were handed down from generation to generation, and it became a core instrument of local folk music. Its spread covers a vast area from sub-Saharan Africa to the Middle East, and it stands as a symbol of cultural connection across regions; it still plays an important role in traditional music performance and everyday life.

The kissar is the traditional lyre of Nubia in East Africa, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.21, a chordophone. The body replaces the traditional turtle-shell back with a shallow round wooden bowl, covered by a goatskin soundboard pierced with two small round soundholes; the arms enter through the soundboard and fan out. Five gut strings are wound on a crossbar and held up by a tailpiece like that of the modern guitar. The right hand plays the melody with a pick while the left hand occasionally plucks a soft drone. It is used in Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea and Ethiopia, and also in the music of Nubia, Shaigiya, Nuba and Beja in northern Sudan.
